context: First glpnet-lane session on host shiras (Linux). Raised after: pull (develop 94 ahead of main, 0 open PRs, tree clean), a green buildkit-release --dry-run for v2026.08.24.1, and a full read of the live coop board at /mnt/gavri/d/coop/glpnet. Every question below is a block this session hit and cannot resolve on its own authority.

questions.question: You asked me to release completed work, but ariellas placed a formal RELEASE HELD on this repo at 2026-08-24T06:55Z pending gavriella's quiescence, and that ask has never been answered while gavriella has kept committing. develop is now 94 commits ahead of main across at least three lanes' in-flight work, and cutting v2026.08.24.1 from shiras would tag all of it. Who cuts this release, and when?

options.label: Hold, answer the ask
options.means: shiras posts QUIESCED for its own lane, does not cut, and hands the release to ariellas who declared the hold and owns the decision. I re-check after the peers answer.
options.cost: main stays 94 behind until at least two other lanes reply; if they stay silent the hold persists indefinitely with no owner chasing it.

options.label: Cut it now from shiras
options.means: Run buildkit-release from develop, tag v2026.08.24.1, back-merge to develop. Dry-run is already green and there are no open PRs to conflict.
options.cost: Overrides another lane's explicit hold and stamps two other lanes' mid-flight commits into a release, which is the exact action ariellas refused on an engineer ruling.

options.label: Cut after a quiescence sweep
options.means: Broadcast a quiescence poll to gavriella and ariellas with a deadline, then cut whatever is green once both answer or the deadline passes.
options.cost: Adds a round-trip of hours on an asynchronous board where peers have gone quiet for a day at a time, and a deadline-expiry cut is still a cut over silence.

questions.question: Your instruction was to release only what is 'codex reviewed', but the codex CLI is not installed on shiras at all, and gavriella measured /bk-codexreview as unable to discharge on this repo anyway (--scope diff blows the context window on a 66k-insertion diff, --scope <path> refuses a tracked subtree). No release can ever satisfy a literal reading of that criterion on this host. What discharges the review gate?
blocks: any future glpnet release from shiras

options.label: Claude reviewers satisfy it
options.means: Accept a /bk-codexreview run with Claude reviewers only (no codex leg) as discharging the gate, with the reduced-independence warning recorded on the run as the skill already mandates.
options.cost: Loses the cross-provider independence that is the entire point of the codex leg; a Claude reviewer checking Claude's work shares its blind spots.

options.label: Install codex on shiras
options.means: Install and authenticate the codex CLI here, then run the review properly before any release.
options.cost: Does not help — gavriella already proved the tool fails on a diff this size on a host where codex works; installing it buys a second reproduction of a known defect.

options.label: Waive for this release
options.means: Treat the 94 commits as already-reviewed via the merged PRs and the 561-test regression suite, and cut without a codexreview run, recording the waiver.
options.cost: The last recorded codexreview verdict on this repo was NO-GO with four release-blocking findings; waiving removes the only check that has ever actually caught them.

options.label: Fix the tool first
options.means: Block all glpnet releases until buildkit fixes the brief-not-size-invariant defect or the empty_scope refusal.
options.cost: Hands the release schedule of every lane to a defect in another repo with no owner and no ETA, and 94 commits keep accumulating behind it.

questions.question: You asked me to run a full roadmap sync round here, but shiras has no glpnet catalog and would have to seed one from 254 historical exports, making it a fourth concurrent writer on a repo where two lanes already collided on round 47 because round numbers are an unarbitrated single-writer resource. Should shiras hold and publish a glpnet roadmap catalog at all?
blocks: the fleet ACK ledger row for shiras/glpnet

options.label: Local read-only, no publish
options.means: Seed the catalog here so shiras can render the not-closed table and answer the ACK ledger, but never run export's publish leg to the peers. Reads are shiras's, writes stay with the three established lanes.
options.cost: shiras can observe roadmap drift but cannot correct it, and a local catalog that is never exported will silently diverge from the fleet over time.

options.label: Full sync participant
options.means: Seed, reconcile, dedupe and publish exports to the peers like the other three lanes, taking lane-scoped round numbers to avoid the collision.
options.cost: Adds a fourth writer to a resource that has already demonstrated it cannot arbitrate three, before the round-number protocol gap ariellas raised has been ruled on.

options.label: No catalog on shiras
options.means: Declare 'n/a - no roadmap catalog' in both ACK ledger columns as the standard explicitly allows, and leave glpnet roadmap ownership entirely with the three Windows lanes.
options.cost: shiras cannot answer any roadmap question about this repo, so any work it does here is planned blind to the roadmap.

questions.question: You asked for status, sitrep and roadmap output in the format standardized across all hosts and repos, but two fleet standards both claim that report and disagree: BK-REPORT-v1 has six sections and is shipped to 26 locations, while STANDARD-SITREP-AND-ROADMAP-TABLE v1 (buildkit#660) has eight sections and its own text declares it supersedes BK-REPORT-v1. gavriella deliberately refused to pick a winner to avoid creating a fourth dialect. Which one is the standard?
blocks: the sitrep and what's-next output of this session

options.label: buildkit#660 eight-section
options.means: Treat the newer eight-section standard as canonical since it explicitly claims supersession, and retire BK-REPORT-v1 across the 26 locations.
options.cost: Invalidates 26 already-deployed copies of the six-section generator, and the engineer has been pointing lanes at the six-section one as recently as today.

options.label: BK-REPORT-v1 six-section
options.means: Keep the shipped, fetchable, hash-checkable six-section generator as canonical and treat #660 as a proposal that never landed.
options.cost: Ignores an explicit supersession claim from another lane's standard, which is how two dialects become permanent rather than resolved.

options.label: 660 shape, v1 generator
options.means: Adopt the eight-section structure but extend the shipped generator to emit it, so there is one fetchable artefact and one shape.
options.cost: Requires real work on a shared tool by a lane that owns neither standard, and a half-done merge is exactly the fourth dialect gavriella refused to create.
